items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 97): You stand on a bathroom scale in an elevator that starts moving downward, travels at a steady speed, and then stops at the bottom. Compare the scale reading with your weight during each part.

question.html: Take up as positive; the scale reads 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔+ 𝑎).

body.html: Starting downward from rest: the velocity is down and growing, so 𝑎< 0 and the scale reads less than your weight. At a steady speed: 𝑎= 0, so it reads your actual weight. Stopping while moving down: the velocity is down but shrinking, so 𝑎 is upward (𝑎> 0) and the scale reads more than your weight.

answer.html: Less than your weight while starting downward, equal to your weight at steady speed, and greater than your weight while stopping.

check.html: Starting down you feel lighter; stopping at the bottom you feel heavier.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 99): A skydiver falling head-first changes to a spread-eagle position. How does this change the drag force at a given speed, and the terminal velocity?

body.html: The drag force depends on speed, size and shape of the object, and on the fluid. Spreading out exposes a larger area to the air.

A larger exposed area gives a larger drag force at any speed. Drag reaches the value of the weight at a smaller speed, so the terminal velocity is lower. The diver controls the fall speed by changing body position.

answer.html: Spreading out increases the area presented to the air, so the drag force at a given speed is larger and the terminal velocity is lower.

items.title: Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 2): A flying squirrel glides from a tall tree to the ground by spreading the loose skin between its legs. What information about forces helps you explain how it controls its speed of descent?

answer.html: Weight (𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔) pulls the squirrel downward, while the drag force exerted by the air opposes the motion and grows with speed. The squirrel speeds up until drag equals weight (terminal velocity, zero net force, constant velocity). Spreading the skin increases surface area, so the drag is larger at any speed and the balance is reached at a lower speed; by changing body shape and angle, the squirrel changes the drag force and so controls its speed.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 27 (Critical Thinking): An airline cargo crew must weigh boxes of produce using only Newton's laws. One calibration box has a known weight of 400 N, and the cargo hold limit is 6000 N in total. The boxes slide on a roller conveyor with very little resistance. Describe how to find each box's weight, and give an example.

body.html: The calibration box has weight 400 N, so its mass is 𝑚<sub>0</sub> = 400 N / 9.8 N/kg = 41 kg. The hold can take 6000 N.

For a (nearly) frictionless horizontal surface 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 𝑚𝑎. If the same horizontal force pushes each box, the masses are in the inverse ratio of the accelerations. Work (method): 1. Push the known 400 N box along the rollers with a steady force 𝐹 (hold a spring scale at one reading), and measure its acceleration 𝑎<sub>0</sub> (for example by timing it from rest over a measured distance, 𝑎= 2𝑑/ 𝑡<sup>2</sup>). 2. Push each unknown box with the same force 𝐹 and measure its acceleration 𝑎. 3. Then 𝑚= 𝐹/ 𝑎, or without knowing 𝐹 at all,

4. Add up the weights and stop loading when the total reaches 6000 N. Example (illustrative numbers): if the calibration box accelerates at 0.60 m/s<sup>2</sup> and another box accelerates at 0.24 m/s<sup>2</sup> under the same force, that box weighs

answer.html: Use the 400 N box to calibrate. Apply the same horizontal force to each other box on the low-resistance rollers, measure the acceleration, and use 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= (400 N)(𝑎<sub>0</sub> / 𝑎) (a smaller acceleration means a heavier box; the example gives 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> N); add the weights to stay under 6000 N.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 99): how wingsuits affect the drag force

body.html: The drag force depends on speed, size and shape of the object, and on the fluid. A wingsuit adds a large surface area between the arms, legs and body.

More surface area means a larger drag force at a given speed. The jumper therefore reaches the speed at which drag equals weight (terminal velocity) sooner and at a smaller value, so the downward speed is lower than for a compact falling body. A jumper can change the drag by changing body shape and orientation, which is how the jumper controls velocity.

answer.html: A wingsuit increases the surface area exposed to the air, which increases the drag force at any given speed, so it lowers the jumper's terminal velocity (and the drag opposes the jumper's motion).

body.html: In spread-eagle fall the diver is at terminal velocity, so 𝐹<sub>drag</sub> = 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>. Opening the parachute suddenly increases the surface area, so drag becomes much larger while velocity has not yet changed.

The diver is still moving downward, so the diver slows down. As the speed falls, drag falls until it again equals the weight at the new, much smaller terminal velocity (about 5 m/s).

answer.html: Yes. The skydiver accelerates upward (an upward acceleration that slows the downward motion) because the drag force now exceeds the weight.

check.html: The small downward acceleration is about 5% of 𝑔, and the reading is about 5% below 9.8 N.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 25: apparent weight on an elevator trip

body.html: Your real weight is always 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔. The apparent weight is the scale (floor) force, 𝐹<sub>scale</sub> = 𝑚(𝑔+ 𝑎) with up positive.

Part of the trip Acceleration Apparent weight versus real weight Going up: starting from the ground floor upward greater Going up: constant speed zero equal Going up: slowing to a stop at the top downward less Going down: starting at the top downward less Going down: constant speed zero equal Going down: slowing to a stop at the bottom upward greater

answer.html: Apparent weight is greater than real weight whenever the acceleration is upward (starting up, stopping on the way down), equal at constant speed, and less whenever the acceleration is downward (stopping at the top, starting down). The three free-body diagrams are shown above: a longer upward arrow, equal arrows, or a shorter upward arrow, each with a downward weight arrow.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 26: Tecle on the ice

body.html: 𝑚= 65.0 kg, 𝐹= 9.0 N (ice is frictionless). Unknown: 𝑎.

answer.html: 𝑎= 0.14 m/s<sup>2</sup> in the direction of the push.

check.html: A small force on a large mass gives a small acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 27 (Critical Thinking): weighing meat crates with Newton's laws

body.html: One crate has a known weight of 1000 N, so its mass is 𝑚<sub>0</sub> = 1000 N / 9.8 N/kg = 102 kg (1.0 × 10² kg). Each truck can hold 10,000 N. The roller belt has very little resistance.

For a (nearly) frictionless horizontal surface 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 𝑚𝑎, so 𝑚= 𝐹/ 𝑎. If the same horizontal force pushes each crate, the masses are in the inverse ratio of the accelerations. Work (method): 1. Push the known 1000 N crate along the roller belt with a steady force 𝐹 (use a spring scale held at one reading), and measure its acceleration 𝑎<sub>0</sub> (for example by timing it over a measured distance from rest, 𝑎= 2𝑑/ 𝑡<sup>2</sup>). 2. Push each unknown crate with the same force 𝐹 and measure its acceleration 𝑎. 3. Then 𝑚= 𝐹/ 𝑎, or without knowing 𝐹 at all,
4. Add up the weights and stop loading when the total reaches 10,000 N. For example (illustrative numbers): if a crate's acceleration is half that of the 1000 N crate, it weighs 2000 N.

answer.html: Use the 1000 N crate to calibrate. Apply the same horizontal force to each other crate on the low-resistance belt, measure the acceleration, and use 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= (1000 N)(𝑎<sub>0</sub> / 𝑎) (a smaller acceleration means a heavier crate); add the weights to stay under 10,000 N.
